requirements.requirement: Separate node2 and node3 onto their own VLANs over the shared link: node2 on VLAN 10, node3 on VLAN 20
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook renders /etc/network/interfaces.d/vlanNN.cfg on ens7 (the shared trunk link), creating ens7.10 with 10.10.10.2/24 on node2 and ens7.20 with 10.10.20.2/24 on node3. Final playbook run and follow-up direct checks confirm both sub-interfaces are up with the correct addresses.

requirements.requirement: Route between the VLANs through node1 (VyOS)
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook configures VyOS eth1 vif 10 (10.10.10.1/24) and vif 20 (10.10.20.1/24) on node1, with kernel IP forwarding confirmed enabled (net.ipv4.ip_forward=1). Interface state and routes were verified both immediately after configuration and after a reboot.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 can still reach each other across the VLANs via node1's routing
requirements.summary: Bidirectional pings between node2 (10.10.10.2) and node3 (10.10.20.2) succeed with 0% loss both immediately after configuration and again after all three nodes (node1, node2, node3) were rebooted, demonstrating the cross-VLAN path survives a restart cycle, aided by a boot-time fixup service that reasserts the VLAN address if the ifupdown/8021q race drops it.

A self-contained Ansible inventory and playbook (/root/vlan-ansible) on the controller (node4) targets vlan_hosts (node2, node3) and router (node1) groups, using raw/command/shell modules (necessitated by the old Python 3.5/2.7 interpreters on the Ubuntu 16.04 hosts breaking normal module execution) to install the vlan package, render interface configs, bring up sub-interfaces, and configure the VyOS router, with assertions verifying the end state.

overall_summary: The executor used Ansible from the controller (node4) to configure 802.1q VLAN sub-interfaces on node2 (VLAN10, ens7.10) and node3 (VLAN20, ens7.20) over the shared trunk link, and configured VyOS node1 as the inter-VLAN router (eth1 vif 10/20) with IP forwarding enabled. End-to-end cross-VLAN reachability between node2 and node3 was directly verified via ping both immediately after configuration and after rebooting all three nodes, confirming the solution survives a restart. The independent provider-wide restart-evidence protocol was executed on all four managed nodes with distinct pre/post boot IDs and confirmed recovery (including the VLAN/routing state on node1-node3), and no post-restart divergence, failed services, or package damage is visible in the fixed lifecycle snapshots.
limitations: Executor command traces are bounded (some ansible-playbook output truncated with 'tail'), so full task-by-task detail of every playbook run is not visible, though the final passing runs and direct verification commands are captured.
No independent probe of node4's own application state (it's the control node with no task-specific role) beyond boot-identity was needed or expected.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most command failures in the trace are discovery/troubleshooting or iterative playbook fixes for real environment quirks (old Python interpreters breaking Ansible's module protocol, an ifupdown/8021q boot race) and were corrected in later runs, leaving no broken final state. During early troubleshooting the executor made several manual, unauthorized-by-playbook mutations directly on node2 outside Ansible control (adding an IP with `ip addr add`, forcing ifdown/ifup) before the working idempotent playbook logic was finalized; these were bounded and fully reverted by a subsequent `ifdown --force` before the final successful Ansible run reconfigured the interface cleanly. The retained systemd 'vlan-fixup.service' unit and helper script on node2/node3 is a deliberate, tested fix for an observed real race condition (verified to run and succeed across a reboot) rather than unrelated scope creep, so it is not treated as unwanted residue. No destructive actions, no weakened security controls, and package/service health snapshots show no failed units or package-manager damage before vs. after.
